results.summary: This is a small game where the player controls a child searching for a ball in a haunted house. Four directional buttons move the character, and an 'Eat' button plus a window action provide additional choices, with LED indicators showing life and ball status. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires two external LEDs for output. Testing involves following the game rules: turning on the life and ball lights, activating only one LED in each of six columns, and avoiding the cake.

This project is a trial logic block for a VGA data controller created for a Tiny Tapeout workshop. It takes two inputs and produces AND and NOR outputs, and is described as having a different clock configuration to test VGA output at various frame rates. The documentation is sparse: it does not explain the VGA interface, the clock settings, or how to connect external hardware, and the 'External hardware' section is left as a placeholder. The design appears to be a simple combinational logic experiment intended for workshop attendees, but its exact purpose and implementation cannot be fully determined from the provided text.

This design implements a simple 3-input majority voting system, where the output goes high if any two or more of the three voter inputs are high. It targets an election-inspired application and is built in Wokwi. The circuit can be tested by connecting three switches to the inputs and an LED to the result output. External hardware includes an LED and switches or pushbuttons. The project is minimal and appears to be an educational example of combinational logic.

This is a 4-bit password security system that grants access for a correct code and triggers a persistent alarm for the trap code 1111. It uses combinational logic for comparison and an SR latch so that the alarm state remains active until a manual reset, demonstrating both combinational and sequential logic in hardware security. The design is implemented in Wokwi. To test it, DIP switches provide the 4-bit input, and LEDs (red and green) plus a buzzer indicate access granted or alarm states. External hardware includes an 8-position DIP switch, pushbuttons for step and reset, LEDs, a buzzer, and resistors. The documentation notes that the circuit processes an 8-bit input in the description despite the 4-bit title, which may be a inconsistency.

This is a 4-digit passcode lock that unlocks only for the code 1010 and activates an alarm for 1111, with a wrong indicator for other codes. It is built from basic logic gates in Wokwi and is combinational, so outputs update directly with inputs. To test it, use DIP switches for the four inputs and observe three LEDs (unlock, wrong, alarm) and a buzzer. External hardware includes a DIP switch, three LEDs, and a buzzer. The design is intended for educational purposes and maps to Tiny Tapeout input/output blocks.

This is a puzzle circuit based on the 'Holidays' Tiny Tapeout example, modified to allow exactly two holiday choices (or an extra sunscreen option). It takes eight inputs and one bidirectional input, and outputs a single logic signal that is true for only specific input combinations. The design is implemented in Wokwi. Testing requires setting the inputs to the specified patterns to get a true output. External hardware is just one LED for output. The documentation lists no other components.

This is a 'live or die' game where a trap is set using DIP switches and loaded into flip-flops, and another player tries to find the trap by pressing check. If the red LED turns on, the player is dead; otherwise, the 'ALIVE' output is indicated. The design is implemented in Wokwi. To test, place the trap with the DIP switch, load it, and then have another player press check. External hardware includes LEDs, a DIP switch, resistors, and pushbuttons. The documentation is very brief and does not detail the exact logic or input/output mapping.

This design is a simple UART transmitter that loads the text 'PSI Open IC 2026' into a shift register and clocks it out to the UART_TX pin. It uses a 100 Hz clock and has control inputs for output enable, reset, and input selection. To test, set RST_N low and provide a clock, then set RST_N high to start transmission; a UART receiver is needed to observe the output. External hardware includes a clock generator and a UART receiver. The design is a straightforward serial communication exercise.

This circuit converts a 4-bit binary-coded decimal (BCD) input (0-9) to 7-segment display outputs, similar to the 7448 IC but with the modification that a zero input always turns the display off. It is implemented in Wokwi. To test, connect four switches to the inputs and a common-cathode 7-segment display to the outputs, then apply valid BCD values from 0 to 9. External hardware includes 4 switches or a DIP switch, a common-cathode 7-segment display, and 7 resistors for protection. The design provides a simple BCD-to-7-segment decoding function.

This project implements a 3-bit magnitude comparator that takes two 3-bit unsigned integers A and B and displays the comparison result on a 7-segment display. The circuit uses XOR gates to detect differences and logic gates to determine greater than, equal, or less than, which are then encoded to drive the display segments. To test, set six switches for A and B, and the display shows the corresponding relationship. External hardware includes a common-cathode 7-segment display connected to the outputs. The design is an educational example of combinational logic and is intended for the IEEE IC Bootcamp at Khalifa University.
